citations.narrative:
Corn crib metal paneling that is used as an enclosure fencing for five ring-tailed lemurs has two inches by four inches
openings. Two of the ring-tailed lemurs can get through the openings of the paneling at will. One lemur was observed
getting out and was fed by members of the public and both lemurs got out, when their enclosure was being observed by
an APHIS Official and the facility representative. This housing facility does not contain all the lemurs securely. Therefore,
the lemurs can be injured from getting out and handling of objects outside of the their enclosure, other animals and
members of the public.
For the prevention of escape and injury, all non-human primate facilities must be constructed to contain and secure the
non-human primates within.
To be corrected by, 30-October-2026.

The outdoor enclosure, housing two spider monkeys, has bedding on the concrete flooring. Approximately 80% of the
bedding is wet and soiled. This contaminated, wet and soiled bedding can attract and provide living areas for insects,
pests and vermin infestation. Similarly, wet and soiled bedding can increase the disease hazards.
For the prevention of disease hazards, insects, pests and vermin, all non-human primate enclosures must have
contaminated and or soiled bedding removed and replace when necessary to satisfy general accepted husbandry
standards.
To be correct by, 29-October-2026.

Two gibbons have a metal shelter inside their enclosure. The tin at the top corner is loose and or is not secure to the
framing. This allows for a sharp edge along the side of the metal tin.
The enclosure, housing five ring-tailed lemurs, has metal tin around the doorway. The top corner of the tin is bent and
protruding outward, thus causing a sharp edge. The lemurs have excess to this edge. There is patch of one inch by one
inch wire along the bottom of the lemur enclosure. This patch is fastened to the corn crib ring paneling. Along the edge of
the wire patch are sharp protruding points. The lemurs have access to these sharp points with their hands and fingers.
The abovementioned sharp edges and points could cause injury to the non-human primates.
For the prevention of injury to non-human primates, all metal surfaces must be repaired and sharp points removed.
To be corrected by, 29-October-2026.

The enclosure housing the two camels has an area of mud and dark brown stagnant water where an enclosure gate and
fence meet. The camels have excess to the muddy stagnant water. This indicates that there is no proper drainage to
rapidly remove water for the outdoor enclosure. If the animals get into the mud, it could increase the disease potential
within their pads and provide living areas for insects that increase disease hazards. Similarly, the camels could be injury
from slipping on the muddy ground.
Approximately 40% of the ground for the grey wolf enclosure is mud. Of this, 15% is brown stagnant water. The two grey
wolves have cake-on mud in their hair coats in areas. This indicates there is no rapid elimination of the water. As a result,
an living area for insects and pests and disease hazards can be increased. Similarly, the wolves cannot remain clean and
dry.
All outdoor enclosures must have a method to rapidly eliminate water. This method shall comply with applicable Federal,
State, and local laws and regulations. As a result, this will prevent muddy areas that could injure the animals, prevent
living areas for insects and decrease disease hazards.
To be corrected by, 01-November-2026.

The grey water bucket used to water the two African porcupines is covered in mud. This indicates the water bucket is not
being kept clean and sanitary. Therefore, the disease hazards for the porcupines can be increased, affecting their health
and comfort.
All watering receptacles must be kept clean and sanitary for the prevention of disease and for the health of the animals.
To be corrected by, 27-October_2026.

The enclosure, housing two Rock Hyraxes, has a pile of animal fecal waste in the corner of the enclosure. The pile was
approximately five inches high and six inches wide at the base. There were flies on the waste pile. This indicates that the
animal waste in the enclosure is not being removed often as necessary to minimize contamination of the animals, and can
increase the disease hazards and orders.
For the minimization of contamination, disease hazards and orders for all animals, excreta must be removed from the
animal enclosures must be removed more often as necessary.
To be corrected by, 24-October-2026.
This inspection and exit interview were conducted with the facility representative.
You may appeal all or part of any inspection report by submitting a written statement contesting the findings—along with
any supporting documentation—to the Deputy Administrator. Appeals of routine, focused, or attempted inspections must
be received within 21 days of report issuance as shown by the signature line of this report.
Appeals may be sent by email to AnimalCare@usda.gov.
Appeals sent by mail should be addressed to:
